overview: This atlas label covers varied Arabian communities from 1492 to 1530, including parts of the central interior and the eastern al-Ahsa oasis region. It is not the name of a single state. Oasis settlements, mobile groups and regional rulers had different institutions; the Jabrids were one important eastern dynasty, not rulers of every place colored here.

periods.title: Regional powers and connections
periods.summary: Jabrid rulers based in eastern Arabia patronized learning and participated in wider pilgrimage and political networks.

periods.title: Upheaval in the east
periods.summary: Muqrin died after fighting the Portuguese in Bahrain in 1521. Jabrid mainland power also broke down during the 1520s.

sections.title: Reading the map and its local societies

items.text: The imported outline includes Hofuf and Diriyah but excludes Mecca, Medina, Jeddah, Julfar and Muscat. It therefore cannot show either all Arab-speaking populations or a unified Arabian kingdom. Examples below name their locations; the pilgrimage-city and seafaring sections describe neighboring connections outside this polygon.

Al-Ahsa was an oasis region with a long agricultural history. Its name is linked to underground accumulations of water. That helps explain why a landscape surrounded by desert could support settled communities as well as connections with mobile neighbors.

The Jabrids were a ruling family centered on al-Ahsa. Ajwad ibn Zamil expanded their influence along the Gulf and exacted tribute from some neighboring rulers. Tribute relationships and local family power made a more complicated political map than one tidy block of color.

Diriyah’s settlement story begins before this map window: in 1446, Mani al-Muraydi moved with his family to Wadi Hanifa. A relative granted him Mulaybid and Ghusaybah. The account distinguishes farmland at Mulaybid from the walled residence and governing center at Ghusaybah: fields and homes were planned together.

Wadi Hanifa’s seasonal floods left fertile silt and replenished groundwater. Traditional agriculture at Diriyah used shallow wells to support orchards and palm groves. A dry-looking valley could thus store part of its usefulness underground, where a farmer with a well could reach it.

Ibn Zayd’s poetry for the Jabrid ruler Ajwad describes camping in al-Dahna after rain and moving to al-Ahsa when dates ripened. This is a court poet’s picture of seasonal life, preserved in later scholarship. It connects desert movement with cultivated palm gardens, rather than treating herding and farming as separate worlds.

The same discussion of Jabrid poetry describes hunting with falcons and cheetahs. These were elite pursuits celebrated in verse, not every child’s afternoon entertainment. The poems offer a lively window into how rulers wanted their outdoor skill and status to be remembered.

At Hofuf, the official heritage account dates al-Jabri Mosque to 1475 and identifies clay and limestone as its building materials. Later repairs repeatedly replaced damaged parts. Its survival is also a story of maintenance: a historic building can carry centuries of careful mending alongside its older fabric.

Al-Ahsa’s broader craft heritage includes pottery made from local clay and ceilings or furniture made with palm trunks and fronds. These are documented regional traditions, not precisely dated inventories of a house in 1500. They show how an oasis could provide building materials as well as food.

Learning could travel with a family. Under Ajwad, Shaykh Nasrullah settled in al-Ahsa to serve as an imam, while the scholarly Abdulqadir family also migrated there. Patronage helped draw teachers into the oasis; political influence was built with books and religious institutions as well as armed followers.

Ahmad ibn Atwa, born at al-Uyaynah in 1456, grew up in a prosperous family that supported his studies. His early education included reading, writing, arithmetic and Quranic recitation. This named scholar’s experience gives us a concrete curriculum, while also reminding us that family resources affected educational opportunities.

Ibn Atwa studied in Damascus, where he lived at al-Umariyah School in 1475 and donated books. He later taught in Najd, including Diriyah at its rulers’ invitation. A student’s journey could therefore become a route by which books, qualifications and teaching practices returned to an Arabian town.
Pilgrimage also carried political connections. In 1520, the Jabrid ruler Muqrin traveled to Mecca, outside this polygon, where Egyptians visited and honored him as an eastern Bedouin leader.

sections.title: Nearby Medina: food, schooling and washing

items.text: A neighboring example comes from Medina, outside the outline. Sultan Qaytbay’s foundation, completed in the 1480s, linked a hostel with eighty cells to a larger religious complex. Its endowment records also describe wheat storage, a mill, bakery and kitchen: supporting visitors required a food supply system, not just a doorway.

At the same Medina foundation, a public water dispenser had a primary school above it. Wheat storerooms and living units shared another building. Lessons, drinking water, supplies and accommodation were brought close together, a very practical arrangement for a busy pilgrimage city.

The Medina hostel complex included an ablution fountain and a small bath. These are specific documented washing facilities, rather than evidence for identical sanitation across Arabia. For a dusty traveler, somewhere to wash was a useful part of hospitality alongside somewhere to sleep.

The navigator Ahmad ibn Majid came from Julfar, outside this polygon, and was associated with the southern Arabian port of al-Shihr. His sailing knowledge belonged to a maritime network. His father and grandfather were also sailors, giving another example of expertise linked to family experience.

Ibn Majid composed both prose manuals and verse about sailing. Historian A. C. S. Peacock suggests that verse helped captains remember instructions. This was practical knowledge about routes, landmarks and stars: rhyme could serve as a memory aid long before a navigator could tap a phone.

An Arabic writing sample is علم البحر, transliterated ʿilm al-baḥr, meaning “knowledge of the sea.” It appears within the Library of Congress’s Arabic title for Ibn Majid’s navigational collection, originally assembled in 1490. The library’s manuscript was copied on 18 June 1926: this is a catalogued later witness to the older work, not a surviving autograph from 1490.

ending.text: The atlas stops this label in 1530, but Arabian communities did not end then. Diriyah’s later history, for example, continued through successive generations and eventually its role as a Saudi capital in the eighteenth century. That later state belongs to a separate historical phase.
